mechanism: Two side-by-side lanes compare host designs: one shared verifier slot, and one slot per login. Each lane ends in a cut-open lock built from login A's challenge, with four pin stacks and an amber shear line; verifier keys have physical teeth. Button 1 starts login B: in the shared lane key B replaces key A, which falls to the plinth, while the per-login rack holds both. Button 2 sends login A's callback: each lane inserts whichever verifier it holds for that slot and the pins rise by that key's teeth. In the per-login lane every pin joint meets the shear line and an amber token rises; in the shared lane after overlap the joints miss the line and no token appears. Sending without starting B passes in both lanes.
spatialBenefit: The comparison is spatial: the same callback reaches two hosts side by side, and the user inspects the cut-open check to see where the mismatch happens (pin joints above and below the line) instead of being told invalid_grant. The user chooses the order, so the failure appears as a race between overlapping logins, a storage bug, rather than as a property of PKCE.
beyondVideoTest: The user controls whether the second login overlaps. Callback first: both lanes pass. Login B first: only the shared slot fails. That counterfactual, plus orbiting to read the misaligned pins inside the section, is not available in a linear video.
interaction: Button: Start login B (disabled after use or after the callback)
Click pins, keys, rack ledges or tokens for one factual sentence
Host Reset restores keys, pins and tokens
expectedObservations: Initially both hosts hold key A; key B is absent.
After Start login B: the shared lane shows key B in the slot and key A on the plinth; the per-login lane shows A and B on separate ledges.
After the callback: per-login pins align and its token rises; shared-lane pins misalign and no token appears.
Callback without overlap: both tokens rise.
sourceGuide: content/concepts/oauth-pkce.json (example: overlapping logins, global verifier overwritten, code A with verifier B fails).
limitations: A pin-tumbler lock is a metaphor for the S256 comparison; the server compares a hash of the verifier with the stored challenge and never sees a key shape.
A passing check is shown as a token; scope, audience and tool permissions remain separate checks the scene does not depict.
Callback binding to the browser session and redirect handling are not shown.
Not yet checked in the integrated browser host.
finalMechanism: None. The lock-and-pin candidate is withdrawn; its runtime assets are left unchanged for the coordinator's records and should not be published.
unsuitabilityEvidence: The lesson's failure is temporal: login B overwrites a shared verifier before callback A arrives. The only reader-controlled variable is event order, which the recommended Sol video already shows with the crossed pair and invalid_grant.

The candidate replacement, per-transaction storage drawers with a tether from state A to verifier A, reduces to a two-row storage table; orbiting or opening drawers adds nothing a labelled diagram does not.

S256 has no honest physical form here: complementary shapes (keys, pins, nesting plates) imply the challenge encodes a recoverable verifier or admits partial matches, which the review rightly flags as a false explanation. An opaque 'press' that emits a fingerprint is a labelled box, i.e. a diagram.
Showing a passing check without implying token issuance requires a further labelled gate for the remaining OAuth checks, adding text choreography the contract excludes.
